question_en: In addition to and separate from its core operations, a global food distributor rents out office complexes that it owns. Last year the company paid total taxes of €15 million, including €3 million in taxes on income from the rentals. Under IFRS, the company's income tax payments would most likely be classified on the company's statement of cash flows as cash flows from:
explanation_en: Under accrual accounting, a company incurs wage expense each period regardless of when wages are actually paid. If actual payment will occur in a later period, the obligation is entered as wages payable—a current liability—on the balance sheet. Wages paid are a component of cash flow from operations (CFO). Calculating CFO using the direct method requires analysis of both the expense and the current liability. Cash paid to employees in any period is a function of wage expense and the change in wages payable for that period. Increasing wages payable means that the company is deferring cash payments until a later period, so the amount of cash paid in the current period decreases. Subtracting this increase from the reported wage expense results in cash paid for wages that is less than the wage expense. This equation has four variables. When three of the four variables are known, the equation can be rearranged algebraically to solve for the unknown: (Choice B) ZAR 25.6 million uses only the wage expense without considering the change in wages payable. (Choice C) ZAR 27.1 million is the result of the change in wages payable being subtracted from—instead of added to—cash wages in the rearranged formula.

(Choice C) Under US GAAP, companies may report dividends paid only under financing activities.

question_en: On its cash flow statement, a company classified its interest paid and interest received as operating activities and classified its dividends paid to shareholders as a financing activity. These classifications are most appropriate under which accounting standard?
explanation_en:
Differences between US GAAP and IFRS for cash flow statement items
US GAAP IFRS
Interest received Operating Operating or investing
Interest paid Operating Operating or financing
Dividend received Operating Operating or investing
Dividend paid Financing Operating or financing
Taxes paid Operating Typically operating, but specific portions can be classified as financing or investing
US GAAP and IFRS have different rules for how certain financial items are classified on a company's statement of cash flows. In general, US
GAAP has more stringent rules and IFRS allows more flexibility. For example, IFRS allows a choice of classification for interest and dividends
(paid or received) and for taxes paid.
In this scenario, the company has classified its interest paid and interest received as operating activities and its dividends paid to shareholders as
a financing activity. These classifications are allowed under both US GAAP and IFRS (Choices A and B).

The amount of the company's ending accounts payable is closest to:
explanation_en:
The amount of cash payments to suppliers is a function of the company's cost of goods sold (COGS), the change in its inventories, and the
change in its accounts payable.
Inventory is a current asset, so purchasing inventory increases assets. If the company buys the inventory on credit instead of paying cash, an

obtained inventory with no cash outlay.

question_en: An analyst compiles the following common-sized cash flow statements as a percentage of revenue for a company: The company had total revenue of MXN 1,000 million in 20X4, MXN 900 million in 20X5, and a tax rate of 20% for both years. The analyst's most appropriate conclusion is that the company is:
option_a: increasing its free cash flow to equity.
option_b: growing its dividend in line with net income.
option_c: expanding its net investments in equipment.
explanation_en: Common-size cash flow statements display each statement item either as a percentage of revenue or as a percentage of the company's total cash inflows or outflows. This allows analysts to compare the receipts and expenditures for companies of different sizes or for one company over time. In this scenario, the common-size cash flow statement indicates that the company's free cash flow to equity (FCFE) as a percentage of revenue increased between 20X4 and 20X5: from 3.5% (= 9% + 5% − 5.5% − 5% + 6% − 6%) in 20X4 to 4.4% (= 11.1% + 6.7% −7.2% − 6.7% + 2.2% − 1.7%) in 20X5. This equates to FCFE of MXN 35 million in 20X4 (= 1,000 × 0.035) and MXN 40 million in 20X5 (= 900 × 0.044). Note: After-tax cash paid for interest is used in the calculation of free cash flow to the firm (FCFF), not FCFE.

question_en: This year, a company has ● £30 million in cash from operations (CFO), ● £6 million in after-tax interest expense that it treats as cash from financing (CFF), ● £2 million in interest received from other companies' bonds that it previously purchased, which it treats as cash from investing (CFI), and ● £15 million in capital expenditures. Under IFRS, the company's free cash flow to the firm (FCFF) is closest to:
explanation_en:
Free cash flow to the firm (FCFF) is the cash available to a firm's providers of capital (eg, lenders and shareholders) after the firm has invested
in long-term assets and working capital. When cash from operations (CFO) is known, the general formula for FCFF simplifies to the column on
the right in the above table.
This question presents an exception to the general rule concerning classification of interest and its impact on FCFF. Interest received or paid is
normally included as CFO. Firms reporting under IFRS may elect to treat interest paid as cash from financing (CFF). If the firm makes this
election, then after-tax interest expense is not added back to CFO, the after-tax interest expense of £6 million is not included in FCFF.
Firms using IFRS may also elect to classify interest received as cash from investing (CFI). Cash interest received is available to the firm's
lenders and shareholders and is added back to CFO if the firm elected to classify it as CFI. The £2 million interest received is included in FCFF,
and the company's FCFF is £17 million as shown below:
(Choice A) £15 million results from correctly omitting the interest paid from the FCFF calculation but fails to add the interest received.
(Choice C) £19 million results comes from adding the after-tax interest expense to CFO. If the company elects to classify interest paid as CFF,
then after-tax interest is not added to CFO.

question_en:
A company reports the following information:

```markdown
| Selected Data (SGD millions) | Prior Year | Current Year |
|---|---|---|
| Net income | 200 | 215 |
| Depreciation | 5 | 5 |
| Interest expense | 20 | 20 |
| Net working capital | 44 | 53 |
| Long-term debt | 300 | 295 |
| Capital expenditures | 40 | 30 |
```

If the company has a 25% tax rate, which of the following cash flow measures is greatest?
option_c: Free cash flow to the firm
explanation_en:
Free cash flow (FCF) determines how much excess cash a company generates from its operations after covering its capital expenditures.
FCF may be used in various ways (eg, reinvesting in the company's business, paying dividends, repaying debt). An analyst can calculate this
cash flow's value to the company's suppliers of debt and equity capital (ie, free cash flow to the firm [FCFF]) or to only equity shareholders (ie, free
cash flow to equity [FCFE]) by adjusting for cash items available to those groups.
FCFF adds back after-tax interest payments since it includes suppliers of debt capital, and interest payments are paid to the company's
debtholders. Since FCFE is available to a company's equity shareholders, it adds back the net borrowing (ie. net change in debt). Companies
may use any additions to debt for the benefit of equity shareholders through dividend payments or share repurchases.
FCF = NI + NCC − ΔWC − ΔFC
= 660 + 260 − 120 − 200 = 600
FCFE = NI + NCC − ΔWC − ΔFC + Net borrowing
= FCF + Net borrowing
= 600 + (535 − 500) = 635
FCFF = NI + NCC − ΔWC − ΔFC + Int (1 − t)
= FCF + Int (1 − t)
= 600 + 40 (1 − 0.25) = 630
In this scenario, the largest measure of FCF is the company's FCFE, which is supported by KRW 40 million in net borrowing (Choices A and C).

question_en: An analyst has gathered the following information for a company's fiscal year 20X9: Based only on this information, under US GAAP, the company's interest coverage ratio is closest to:
explanation_en:
The interest coverage ratio, one of the tools used to determine a company's ability to service its debt, is a measure of firm solvency. It is
usually calculated (using the income statement) as the ratio of EBIT to interest expense.
When using a cash flow statement prepared under US GAAP, the interest coverage ratio is CFO plus back interest and taxes paid (similar to EBIT)
divided by interest paid. Adding back interest and taxes paid is necessary since net income (ie, net of interest and tax expense) is the starting
point for operating cash flow.
Under IFRS, if interest paid is classified as a financing activity, that portion of interest paid should not be added back to the numerator to determine
interest coverage.
(Choice A) 3.6 times coverage is the result if interest paid is subtracted from the numerator.
(Choice C) 5.9 times coverage is the result if all cash flow metrics (ie, CFO, cash flow from investing [CFI], cash flow from financing [CFF]) are
included in the numerator.

question_en:
An analyst reviews the following common-sized cash flow statement:

| Cash Flow From Operating Activities | Percentage of Net Revenue (20X7) |
|---|---|
| Net income | 20.00 |
| Depreciation | 7.00 |
| Change in accounts receivable | (9.00) |
| Change in inventory | (6.00) |
| Change in accounts payable | 8.50 |
| Net cash provided by operating activities | 20.50 |

Which of the following best describes the impact on net cash provided by operating activities?
option_a: The increase in inventory decreases cash flow
option_b: The decrease in accounts payable increases cash flow
option_c: The decrease in accounts receivable decreases cash flow
explanation_en:
Common-sized cash flow statements may be reported as a percentage of net revenue. Increases in assets indicate a use of cash and are
shown as negative numbers on a common-sized cash flow statement; decreases are shown as positive figures. In this question, inventory is
increasing, so it decreases cash flow and is shown as a negative percentage of net revenue. Increases in liabilities suggest a source of cash.
Increases in liabilities are shown as positive figures and decreases as negative figures on common-sized statements of cash flow.
(Choice B) Accounts payable increases when a company purchases assets on credit and decreases as the company pays off those assets. It is
the increase, not the decrease, in accounts payable that increases cash flow.
(Choice C) Accounts receivable increases when a company extends credit to customers and decreases when the company collects cash from
them. It is the increase, not the decrease, in accounts receivable that decreases cash flow.

subtopic: 5.06 Analysis of Inventories
question_en: An automotive parts company manufactures specialty engine pistons and presents its financial statements using US GAAP. Due to manufacturing improvements, it estimates that its inventory is worth less than its carrying value. The relevant per-unit information for 20X8 is shown below: If this company uses LIFO, the per-unit cost for its 20X8 ending inventory is closest to:
explanation_en: US GAAP require companies using LIFO to report inventory at the lower of cost or market value. US GAAP define market value as replacement cost, subject to upper and lower limits. The upper limit is net realizable value (ie, the selling price less costs to complete and sell the inventory). The lower limit is net realizable value minus a normal profit margin. The company's original cost is $105 per unit, which is higher than the $90 replacement cost, so this company must write down its inventory to market value. "Market value" is a range defined by the upper limit of net realizable value ($100) (Choice C) and the lower limit of net realizable value minus a normal profit margin ($100 - $7 = $93). The actual replacement cost ($90) is less than the lower limit ($93), so the company can write down its inventory to only $93 per unit. (Choice A) This is the company's actual replacement cost, but since it is less than the GAAP-specified lower limit of net realizable value minus a profit margin, the company cannot reduce the inventory value below the lower limit of $93 per unit.

subtopic: 5.06 Analysis of Inventories
question_en: In a period of increasing inventory costs, a company using FIFO instead of LIFO will most likely experience a lower:
explanation_en: Changing inventory unit costs have different effects on a company's reported financials, depending on its inventory valuation method. With the FIFO method, the oldest units purchased are used in the calculation of cost of goods sold (COGS) whereas the most recent additions are used to value inventory. During periods of rising inventory costs, the most expensive units "remain" in inventory whereas the least expensive units are used for COGS. In comparison, a company using LIFO experiences a larger COGS and smaller inventory. A company's inventory turnover ratio measures its efficiency in managing its inventories. In periods of rising inventory costs, a company reporting with the FIFO method instead of LIFO will report lower COGS, which is the numerator of the inventory turnover ratio, and higher inventory, which is the denominator. Therefore, the company's inventory ratio will be lower using FIFO compared to LIFO. (Choice A) Current ratios are higher for companies reporting in FIFO during periods of rising inventory costs, since inventories are larger and current liabilities are unchanged. (Choice B) Gross profit margins are higher for companies using FIFO during periods of rising inventory costs, since a lower COGS results in a higher gross profit and revenue remains unchanged.

With very few exceptions, upward revaluation is limited to the amount of all previous write-downs. Further, the maximum value for the inventory is its original cost. subtopic: 5.06 Analysis of Inventories
question_en: A clothing retailer reporting under IFRS purchased merchandise for £500,000 at the beginning of the year. Normally, the retailer could sell this inventory for £700,000, but now the estimated selling price is £510,000. The cost of selling the inventory is £15,000. Based on this information, the retailer's reported carrying value of inventory (in £ thousands) is closest to:
explanation_en: FIFO (first-in, first-out) inventory costing means that a company is deemed to have sold its older inventory first. When inventory costs fall, older inventory is valued higher than more recently purchased inventory. The older inventory is included in the cost of goods sold (COGS), so a higher- valued inventory equals higher COGS. Gross profit is the difference between revenues and COGS, so a higher COGS translates to lower profits. When older inventory is sold first, ending inventory consists of the more recent purchases. With falling inventory costs, more recent purchases are less costly than the older ones, so ending inventory is worth less than beginning inventory. Inventory is a current asset, and the current ratio is calculated as current assets divided by current liabilities. A lower ending inventory value means a lower value for both current assets and the current ratio. (Choice B) Since COGS is higher when inventory costs fall (using FIFO), gross profit is lower, not higher. The gross profit margin is equal to gross profit divided by revenues, so the gross profit margin is also less. (Choice C) Working capital is the difference between current assets and current liabilities. A lower inventory value results in lower working capital.

subtopic: 5.06 Analysis of Inventories
question_en: .A company reporting under US GAAP and using FIFO assesses its inventory's net realizable value as being €200,000 less than its carrying value. The company records a write-down and increases COGS by €200,000. In the subsequent period, a new assessment of the inventory's net realizable value is €250,000 higher than its revised carrying value. The company's most appropriate action is to reduce COGS by:
explanation_en: Companies write down the carrying value of inventory on the books due to spoilage, obsolescence, or reductions in selling prices. When a write-down occurs, the company decreases inventory on the balance sheet and increases COGS on the income statement, both by the amount of the write-down. These adjustments have a negative impact on liquidity and profitability ratios and an artificially positive impact on activity ratios. Activity ratios measure efficiency. One common example is inventory turnover (or COGS / Inventory), which measures the average number of times a company sells its average inventory over a period. After a write-down, the ratio becomes higher since an inventory write-down increases COGS (numerator) and decreases inventory (denominator). This makes a company appear to be more efficient at turning its inventory into sales. Analysts should be aware of the impact of such practices and make appropriate adjustments when analyzing financial reports. (Choice B) Liquidity ratios measure a company's ability to cover short-term obligations. They commonly consist of current assets (including inventory) in the numerator and current liabilities in the denominator. Decreasing inventory value reduces the numerator, which worsens the ratio. (Choice C) Profitability ratios measure a type of profit as a fraction of revenue. Write-downs increase COGS, an expense, thereby decreasing all types of profitability.

question_en: A company that reports under US GAAP decides to change its inventory accounting from FIFO to LIFO. The change on its financial statements is most appropriately disclosed:
option_a: retroactively, including a restatement of prior years' financial statements.
option_b: retroactively, without restating prior financial statements but disclosing the impact of the change to prior years' statements in footnotes.
option_c: prospectively, without restating prior financial statements but disclosing the impact of the
explanation_en: Inventory constitutes a large percentage of total assets for many companies and can significantly impact revenue, expenses (ie, cost of sales), and liquidity. As such, companies provide inventory-related disclosures in financial statements to better explain reporting methods and trends. One important category of disclosure relates to reversals of previously written down inventory, which is permitted under IFRS only. In general, a write-down occurs when an inventory item's market value falls below its carrying value on the balance sheet. A write-down increases expenses (cost of sales) and lowers profits. Any subsequent reversals of write-downs will allow companies to recapture these lost profits. (Choice A) LIFO reporting is allowed under US GAAP, not IFRS. LIFO reserves measure the difference between ending inventory value measured under FIFO and LIFO and are reported only for US GAAP companies. (Choice B) Companies using both US GAAP and IFRS disclose information related to inventory write-downs.

subtopic: 5.06 Analysis of Inventories
question_en: A manager collects information on a company's inventory for a period: The company uses LIFO to calculate COGS. Based on only this information, under US GAAP, the per-unit value (in USD) for the existing inventory is closest to:
explanation_en:
Inventory may lose value due to spoilage, obsolescence, or declines in selling prices. Companies often update their inventory values on the
balance sheet to account for such events. US GAAP require companies to report inventory at the lower of historical cost or market value (MV).
When a company reports under US GAAP and uses LIFO as its inventory costing method, MV is the current replacement cost subject to an
upper and lower limit.
The upper limit is the net realizable value (NRV), which is the selling price net of the costs to complete and sell the inventory. In this
scenario, NRV = Selling price − Selling cost − Completion cost, so NRV = 140 − 10 − 30 = 100.
The lower limit is the NRV minus a normal profit margin. In this scenario, the lower limit is NRV − Normal profit margin = 100 − 7 = 93.
MV is always the middle number of the replacement cost (RC), upper limit, and lower limit when ranked in order:
If RC > Upper > Lower, MV is the upper limit.
If Upper > RC > Lower, MV is the RC.
If Upper > Lower > RC, MV is the lower limit.
In this case, the MV is the RC of $96 per unit since it is within the upper and lower limits and is lower than the historical cost of the inventory.
(Choice B) $100 is the upper limit for MV, which is capped at the upper limit only when RC exceeds the upper limit.
(Choice C) $105 is the company's historical cost. The inventory's NRV is lower than its historical cost, so the NRV should be reported.

question_en: In 20X7, a company wrote down its inventory from £30 million to £28.7 million. In 20X8, a global shortage of this product results in the inventory having a net realizable value of £35 million. Under IFRS, the company's revaluation of inventory to reflect its increased value is closest to:
explanation_en:
Inventory write-downs and revaluations
US GAAP IFRS
Lower of cost or net realizable value (FIFO) Lower of cost or net realizable value (LIFO not permitted
Lower of cost or market value (LIFO) under IFRS)
Market value equals replacement cost but with an upper and lower limit Revaluations in future periods permitted
Upper limit: net realizable value Revaluations limited to amount of all previous write-
Lower limit: net realizable value less normal profit margin downs (except for agricultural, forest, and mineral
Revaluations generally NOT permitted products)
IFRS, unlike GAAP, permit upward revaluation of inventory if the net realizable value increases. With very few exceptions, upward revaluation
is limited to the amount of all previous write-downs. Further, the maximum value for the inventory is its original cost.
This company wrote down its inventory by £1.3 million to reflect its reduced value. Although the value has sharply increased, the amount of
revaluation is limited to the previous £1.3 million reduction. This brings the inventory's value back to its original cost of £30 million.
(Choice A) This would be the case under US GAAP, which do not permit upward revaluations to previously written-down inventory except for
agricultural, forest, and mineral products.
(Choice C) IFRS limit revaluation of inventory to the original cost, even if the future net realizable value exceeds the original cost. For
agricultural, forest, and mineral products, revaluations can exceed the original cost.
